newsitem.title: USA: NY precious metals lower, gold off on Belgian news.
newsitem.headline: NY precious metals lower, gold off on Belgian news.

text.p: COMEX and NYMEX precious metals futures were lower midday Wednesday, with gold slipping back from a firmer opening, on news the Belgian government proposed selling more of its gold reserves by means of additional issues of commemorative gold coins from 1999 onwards.
COMEX August gold was down $1.00 at $342.70 an ounce, with the weak downtrend since early May still seen intact, though support has held three times around $343.00 an ounce.
In the bullion market, spot gold was quoted $340.70/20 early, compared to the London Wednesday afternoon fix at $341.60 and the New York close Tuesday around $341.50/00.

Belgian central bank officials said Wednesday the Belgian government has proposed increasing the amount of central bank gold that can be sold as commemorative gold coins to 26 tonnes a year from 1999 onwards, up to a maximum of 133 tonnes.

Currently the National Bank of Belgium is authorized to sell up to 2.75 pct of its 1987 gold reserves in the form of coins, and the new proposal is to increase the amount authorized to 10 pct of the 1987 reserves.
At the start of 1987 the Belgian central bank held 1,329 tonnes of gold, but had sold 733 tonnes by the end of 1996.
The proposed extra sales of coins would allow Belgium to pay down more of its debt which stands at 129 pct of GDP, the highest debt-to-GDP ratio in the EU.
But the plan must still obtain parliamentary approval and would also be subject to approval by the new European Central Bank (ECB) which is due to be operational from January 1999.

"I dont believe the Belgian government will be able to sell that amount of gold in commemorative coins," said Leonard Kaplan, a broker with MONEX, one of the largest U.S. retailers of gold investment products.

Total world sales of major bullion coins (Krugerrand, American Eagle, Austrian Philharmonic, Canadian Maple Leaf, Australian Nugget, English Britannia) in 1996 amounted to 36.8 tonnes, according to the latest World Gold Council survey.
"But central banks are looking for a method of disposing of more of their gold reserves, so this kind of thing will only happen more often," Kaplan said.
On another negative note, the Swiss parliament Wednesday approved a revised charter for the Swiss central bank, allowing it to start lending gold to improve its earnings.
The charter also reduced the amount of gold the Swiss National Bank must hold to cover its notes in circulation to 25 percent from 40 percent.
COMEX July silver was down 5.7 cents at $4.705 an ounce midday, reversing Tuesday's gains.
July silver has been in a $4.65-4.90 range since mid-May, with good industrial demand seen below $4.70 and ample supply seen near $4.90, analysts said.

Silver is still seen having better fundamentals than gold, without the overhang of potential central bank sales to cap the market, as silver enters the ninth year of a shortfall between world silver mine production and fabrication demand.
NYMEX July platinum was down $3.60 at $407.50 an ounce, while NYMEX September palladium was off $6.40 at $171.50, after execution of a large stop order at $170.00, traders said.
Funds were continuing to liquidate long positions in July platinum ahead of the contract's delivery period starting in two weeks, traders said.
In the physical market, one month lease rates for platinum remained around 50 pct and for palladium around 100 pct, while the market waited for Russian supplies resume in late June.

In overnight news, the Tokyo Commodity Exchange (TOCOM) said it was in discussions with the London Platinum and Palladium Market Association about restoring orderly trading conditions to the PGM market.
The London Platinum and Palladium Market had also contacted the New York Mercantile Exchange (NYMEX), TOCOM officials said.
((Clive McKeef, New York Commodities Desk, 212-859-1641))
